title: Before You Marry
subtitle: Eight conversations for two people thinking about forever, to have alongside premarital counseling: your families, your faith, how you fight, money, sex, children, and the vows.
audience: engaged couples and couples seriously considering marriage, and the pastors and mentors who meet with them
intro:
If you're holding this, you're probably thinking about forever. Maybe you're engaged and the date is set, and the weeks are filling up with guest lists and deposits. Maybe there's no ring yet, but you've started saying *when* instead of *if*. Either way, it's easy to spend more hours planning a wedding than talking about a marriage. The wedding is a day. The marriage is the rest of your lives, and it will be built out of conversations you have now or have later, when they're harder.

This workbook holds eight of those conversations, the ones couples tend to put off until after the wedding: why marry at all, the families you come from, what you believe about God, how you fight, money, sex, who does what, children, and the promises themselves. None of it is a test, and nobody hands you a score. But it may show you something you didn't know about each other, or about yourself, and it's far kinder to find that at a kitchen table than in the second year of a marriage.

It's written by a pastor, and it doesn't hide that. Every session prints Scripture in full and takes it seriously, because Christians believe marriage was God's idea before it was ours. If one of you doesn't share that belief, you're welcome here. No one will ask you to pretend, and nothing in these pages is a trick to sign you up for something. At the very least you'll learn what the person you love believes they're promising, and that's worth knowing before either of you promises anything.

This workbook can't tell you whether to marry. Only the two of you can decide that, before God and alongside people who know you both. What it can do is help you decide with your eyes open. Plenty of people have made vows without knowing what they were promising, and God has been kind to many of them. You have the chance to know first. It won't come twice.
howToUse:
Take one session at a time, a week or two apart, and start months before the wedding rather than weeks, so there's time to act on what you find. Print a copy for each of you, because the questions are answered alone. Each session opens with why it matters and Scripture printed in full; read those aloud together. Then go to separate rooms and write your answers, briefly and honestly, before you talk. Come back together for the conversation, and choose the one thing you'll do before the next session.

Write what's true, not what you think the other wants to read, and write *I don't know* when you don't. Your written answers belong to you, so share what you're ready to share. If a conversation turns into a fight you can't finish, stop, and bring it to the next session or to your pastor. If you ever find you can't write an honest answer because you're afraid of how the other will react, stop the workbook altogether. That fear is an answer, and the note just below says what to do with it.

Pastors and mentors: this is meant to go alongside your meetings with a couple, not to replace them. Meet with each person alone at least once, and ask whether they ever feel afraid, pressured, or controlled. If either says yes, don't counsel them together, don't repeat what you heard to the other, and help the one who is afraid reach the Hotline. Where a session reaches a question faithful Christians answer differently, such as the roles of husband and wife, birth control, or remarriage after divorce, the workbook sets out each view as its own defenders would and sends the couple to you and their church to settle it.
careNote:
This workbook is for two people who are safe with each other, and consent between you is never optional, before the wedding or after it. If either of you is afraid of the other, or feels controlled, watched, threatened, or pressured, including sexually, stop here, and don't do couples work with a partner you fear. Talk alone with someone you trust, and call or text the National Domestic Violence Hotline in the box below. If anyone is in immediate danger, call 911.

A workbook is not a substitute for meeting with a pastor or a premarital counselor. Anything that surfaces about past abuse, addiction, trauma, or a struggle with mental health deserves its own help from a licensed counselor, not only a conversation between the two of you. Nothing here is medical, legal, or financial advice.
closing:
If you've come this far, you've had conversations many couples never have, and you know each other better than when you began. Now there's a decision in front of you, and it belongs to the two of you, before God.

If these sessions showed you something that needs more time, take the time. A wedding can be moved. If they showed you that you shouldn't marry, that's a grief, and an honest one, and you don't owe everyone an explanation. Talk with your pastor, and let your friends carry you for a while. If what you found is fear, talk with the Hotline at the front before you end things; leaving a controlling partner can be dangerous, and they can help you plan it safely.

If you're going ahead, keep this workbook and come back to it on your anniversaries. Your answers will change, and some of these questions will mean more in the tenth year than in the first.

You'll break these promises in small ways, probably within the first year. The marriages that last are made of two people who failed each other and kept coming back. What finally holds them is God's faithfulness more than theirs. He has kept covenant with people who didn't keep theirs, and in Christ he gave himself up for a church that wasn't yet holy. That's the love you're promising to imitate, and it's the love that will hold you when you can't.

The LORD has been a witness between you through every page of this workbook. He'll be there when you make your vows, and on some ordinary Tuesday years from now, when one of you has to decide, again, to keep them.

sessions.title: Why marry at all?
sessions.why:
First, one thing has to be said plainly: this workbook assumes two people who are safe with each other. If either of you is afraid of the other, or feels controlled, watched, threatened, or pressured, including sexually, stop here, and don't do couples work of any kind with a partner you fear. Talk alone with someone you trust, and call the National Domestic Violence Hotline, listed at the front of this workbook under *If anyone is in danger*. In immediate danger, call 911. Everything after this assumes you're safe.

Plenty of thoughtful people wonder why anyone should marry at all. If you love each other, what does a license add, or a wedding? Some of that suspicion is earned, and the church has earned its share. A ceremony can't make love, and many marriages have been lonely or cruel behind good photographs. But the question treats marriage as a way of certifying a feeling, and Scripture describes something sturdier.

In Genesis, before anything has gone wrong, God names one thing that isn't good: the man is alone. None of the animals the man names is a fit companion for him, and when God brings the woman, the first words Scripture gives him are a song. Then a man leaves his father and mother to be united to his wife, and two people stand naked and unashamed, fully known and unafraid of being known. Centuries later the prophet Malachi told the men of Judah, weeping at the altar because God no longer accepted their offerings, that the LORD had witnessed their covenant with the wives of their youth, the companions they'd broken faith with. God had been in the room the whole time.

A contract trades goods and services and ends when one side stops delivering. A covenant binds persons. It's a promise to keep faith with someone even when they can't give you anything back, made before God, who keeps his own promises that way. Love makes two people want to promise. The promise is what carries them through the years when wanting isn't enough.

scripture.text: The LORD God also said, “It is not good for the man to be alone. I will make for him a suitable helper.” And out of the ground the LORD God formed every beast of the field and every bird of the air, and He brought them to the man to see what he would name each one. And whatever the man called each living creature, that was its name. The man gave names to all the livestock, to the birds of the air, and to every beast of the field. But for Adam no suitable helper was found. So the LORD God caused the man to fall into a deep sleep, and while he slept, He took one of the man’s ribs and closed up the area with flesh. And from the rib that the LORD God had taken from the man, He made a woman and brought her to him. And the man said: “This is now bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh; she shall be called ‘woman,’ for out of man she was taken.” For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and they will become one flesh. And the man and his wife were both naked, and they were not ashamed.

And this is another thing you do: You cover the altar of the LORD with tears, with weeping and groaning, because He no longer regards your offerings or receives them gladly from your hands. Yet you ask, “Why?” It is because the LORD has been a witness between you and the wife of your youth, against whom you have broken faith, though she is your companion and your wife by covenant.

questions: Picture an ordinary weeknight ten years into your marriage. What are you doing, and what are you worried about?
What are you hoping marriage will give you that you don't have now? Is there anything you're hoping it will fix?
Which marriage that you've watched up close makes you want to marry? Which one makes you afraid to, and what exactly are you afraid of?
A friend tells you marriage is just paperwork. What would you say is the real reason you want to marry, rather than keep things as they are?
If your partner became seriously ill, or failed at something that mattered to you both, what would keep you there? Write the honest answer, not the expected one.
Is there anything about you that the person you plan to marry doesn't know yet and should? You don't have to write what it is. Write what it would cost to tell.
Whose opinion of your relationship would you take seriously, and what do you think they would honestly say about it?
sessions.together:
Read Genesis 2:18-25 aloud again and stay with the last verse. Talk about what it would take for each of you to be fully known by the other and not ashamed, and what you're most afraid the other might find out. You don't have to tell everything tonight. Agree on what needs telling before the wedding, and when.

Then trade answers to the first four questions, and listen for what surprises you. If your pictures of an ordinary weeknight look nothing alike, don't panic. You've found your first real conversation.

Last, each of you name three things you expect from the other in marriage. Take them one at a time, and each ask yourself honestly: if my partner couldn't give me this for a year, through illness or failure, would I stay? This is about what illness or failure might take from you, never about harm. The answers will show you where your love still works like a contract. Everyone's does, somewhere. Better to find the place now, while you can still talk about it.
sessions.practice: If it's safe and possible, ask a parent or the adult who raised you how they met, what they promised each other, and what they wish they'd known at your age. Listen more than you comment. If that conversation isn't possible or wouldn't be safe, write down what you know of their story and what you've only been able to guess. Bring both to the next session.

sessions.title: Where we come from
sessions.why:
When you marry, you marry a history along with a person. Each of you grew up in a home that taught you, mostly without words, how people argue or go quiet, how money is spent or hidden, how love is shown, and whether anyone says sorry. It will surface first in small things, a holiday plan or a sink full of dishes, because small things are where habits live.

Genesis says a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife. You're still to honor your parents (Exodus 20:12), but leaving moves your first loyalty. Your parents become people you love and consult; your spouse should never have to compete with them. For some of you, the family that's hardest to leave is a hurt one, and a hurt family can follow you across a state line.

God's people in Ezekiel's day had a proverb for this: the fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth were set on edge. They used it to blame the generation before them, and God refused it. Ezekiel pictures a son who sees all his father's sins, considers them, and does not do likewise, and God says he will surely live. Your family explains a great deal about you, but it doesn't get to decide who you become.

Some of you grew up without a father, or watched your parents' marriage end, or lived with addiction or violence. I was raised without a father, so I won't treat this as a footnote. Promises a child makes in pain, about what they'll never repeat, are hard to keep well: some people end up repeating the very thing, and others swing so far from it that the swing does its own damage. If what you carry includes abuse, it deserves a licensed counselor's help, not only this conversation. Psalm 68 calls God a father of the fatherless, who settles the lonely in families. The home you're building can be one of the ways he does it.

scripture.text: What do you people mean by quoting this proverb about the land of Israel: ‘The fathers have eaten sour grapes, and the teeth of the children are set on edge’? As surely as I live, declares the Lord GOD, you will no longer quote this proverb in Israel. ... Now suppose this son has a son who sees all the sins his father has committed, considers them, and does not do likewise ... Such a man will not die for his father’s iniquity. He will surely live.

A father of the fatherless, and a defender of the widows, is God in His holy habitation. God settles the lonely in families; He leads the prisoners out to prosperity, but the rebellious dwell in a sun-scorched land.

questions: When the adults in your home disagreed, what happened? Who raised their voice, who went quiet, and how did it usually end?
How was love shown in your family, and how was it withheld? Did approval have to be earned, and how?
What did your family teach you about money or about God without ever saying it out loud?
What did you promise yourself, as a child or a teenager, that you would never do or never allow in your own home?
Which habit of your partner's family do you already find hard? Write it as honestly and as kindly as you can.
When your family and your partner want different things, whose side do you expect to take? Whose side have you actually taken so far?
If you've been married before or have a child from an earlier relationship, what are you still carrying from it that your partner needs to understand?
sessions.together:
Trade answers to the first and fourth questions. Then sketch both families on one sheet, back to your grandparents, marking the marriages that lasted and the ones that ended, the absences, the addictions, and the places faith was real. Each of you name one thing you want to carry forward and one thing you want to end with you.

Where will you spend the holidays? How much will your parents hear about your disagreements?

If either of you has been married before, faithful churches answer differently whether a divorced Christian may marry again. Some hold that marriage binds until death. Paul, passing on the Lord's command, tells a wife who separates to remain unmarried or be reconciled (1 Corinthians 7:10-11), and Mark and Luke record Jesus' teaching on remarriage with no exception (Mark 10:11-12; Luke 16:18). Their comfort is a vow that holds the way God's promises hold. Others hold that sexual immorality or desertion frees the wronged spouse to marry again, reading the exception Jesus names in Matthew 19:9 and Paul's word that a believer whose unbelieving spouse leaves is not bound (1 Corinthians 7:15), and some extend that to abuse. Their comfort is that the one betrayed or abandoned is free to begin again. Both guard something true: the permanence of the promise, and the protection of the betrayed. Settle it with your pastor and your church before you set a date.
sessions.practice: If you can do it honestly and safely, thank a parent or the adult who raised you for one specific thing they gave you that you want to carry into your marriage. Honest gratitude is one way to honor a parent, and it doesn't require pretending the rest didn't happen. If no one in your family comes to mind, think of whoever did give you something, a grandparent, a coach, a teacher, or a neighbor, and tell your partner who it was and what it was.

sessions.title: What we believe
sessions.why:
Two people can sit in the same pew for years and believe quite different things. One of you may pray every day and the other only in emergencies. You may come from churches that baptize or worship differently. One of you may not believe at all, or may believe less than the other assumes. Couples often steer around this because it feels private or likely to start a fight, but what you believe about God will shape your Sundays, your giving, your forgiving, and what you teach your children.

If you're the one who doesn't believe, you may be here because someone you love asked you to come. You're welcome, and these pages won't push you. I came to faith from atheism, and I'd rather you tell the truth about what you believe than say what the room wants to hear. Faith professed to clear the way to a wedding isn't faith, and it isn't fair to either of you. In the passage printed here, Nathanael's first words about Jesus are a sneer, and Jesus' first words about Nathanael praise his honesty.

If you're the one who believes, the plainest instruction the New Testament gives about whom to marry is Paul's: anyone you wish, as long as they belong to the Lord. He wrote it about widows, and many Christians since have taken it as the rule for every believer who marries. You may know the verse about being unequally yoked; it comes in a passage calling a church away from idolatry (2 Corinthians 6:14-16), and many apply it to marriage as well. Neither verse is a verdict on your partner's worth. Both are about what a marriage stands on. Hoping a wedding will bring someone to faith asks love to do what only God can, and it turns the person you love into a project.

scripture.text: Philip found Nathanael and told him, “We have found the One Moses wrote about in the Law, the One the prophets foretold—Jesus of Nazareth, the son of Joseph.” “Can anything good come from Nazareth?” Nathanael asked. “Come and see,” said Philip. When Jesus saw Nathanael approaching, He said of him, “Here is a true Israelite, in whom there is no deceit.”
A wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives. But if her husband dies, she is free to marry anyone she wishes, as long as he belongs to the Lord.

questions: What do you actually believe about God right now? Write it in your own words, doubts included.
How did you come to believe what you believe, or to stop believing? Who or what had the most to do with it?
What part do you want faith to play in an ordinary week of your marriage: on Sundays, at meals, with money, on hard days?
If you have children, what do you want them taught about God, and by whom?
Have you said you believe something, or agreed to something about church, mainly to keep the peace with your partner or their family?
How would you feel if your partner's faith grew much stronger after the wedding? How would you feel if it faded?
If you don't share the same faith, what would you be giving up by marrying, and what would you be asking the other to give up?
sessions.together:
Tell each other the story of your faith, or of your unbelief, as honestly as you can. The listener's job is to understand, not to correct or persuade, and to ask one question that shows they were listening.

If you both believe, talk about what faith will look like in your home: which church you'll belong to, whether and when you'll pray together, how you'll spend Sundays, and what you'll do when one of you drifts. Praying together out loud can feel awkward at first. Start small, and start anyway.

If one of you believes and the other doesn't, this is the hardest conversation in the workbook, and it should be. Talk honestly about what 1 Corinthians 7:39 means for the decision in front of you, with no pressure in either direction, and then, if you're both willing, take that conversation to a pastor together. Don't try to settle it in one night. And if you're the one who doesn't believe but would like to look at the faith for yourself, with no one watching, there's a page written for you at livewellbyjamesbell.co/help/curious.
sessions.practice: If you both believe, pray together out loud for a few minutes at least three times before the next session, even if it feels clumsy, and notice what makes it hard. If one of you doesn't believe, don't force that. The one who believes can pray alone, and if you're both willing, the two of you can set a time to talk with a pastor about what you're deciding.

sessions.title: How we talk, and how we fight
sessions.why:
Every couple disagrees. What matters is how you fight when you do, and whether you find your way back afterward. A couple who never argue have often just settled that one of them will stay quiet, and the quiet one tends to pay for it later. A disagreement handled well can bring two people closer. One handled badly, again and again, teaches both of you that it's safer to stop telling the truth.

The letter of James asks everyone to be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger. It doesn't forbid anger outright, but it warns that human anger won't produce the righteousness God desires, and it puts listening first. The letter to the Ephesians, written to people who belonged to one another, comes at the same thing from another side. It tells them to put off falsehood and speak the truth, to be angry without sinning and not let the sun go down on it, since anger kept overnight gives the devil a foothold, to say only what builds up, and to put bitterness away and forgive as God in Christ forgave them.

Draw one line clearly. Conflict is two people who disagree and are both free to speak. Control is one person running the other's life: deciding whom they may see and what they may spend, checking their phone, punishing with silence, making them afraid. Fear is the sign. If you're afraid of your partner, or you find yourself managing their moods to stay safe, better listening won't fix it. Stop the workbook, talk alone with someone you trust, and call the Hotline listed at the front.

For two people who are safe with each other, repair matters as much as restraint. Some of us learned at home that a fight ends when everyone pretends it didn't happen. A fight isn't over when the shouting stops. It's over when you've come back to each other, said what was true, owned what was wrong, and forgiven.

scripture.text: My beloved brothers, understand this: Everyone should be quick to listen, slow to speak, and slow to anger, for man’s anger does not bring about the righteousness that God desires.

Therefore each of you must put off falsehood and speak truthfully to his neighbor, for we are all members of one another. “Be angry, yet do not sin.” Do not let the sun set upon your anger, and do not give the devil a foothold. ... Let no unwholesome talk come out of your mouths, but only what is helpful for building up the one in need and bringing grace to those who listen. And do not grieve the Holy Spirit of God, in whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. Get rid of all bitterness, rage and anger, outcry and slander, along with every form of malice. Be kind and tenderhearted to one another, forgiving each other just as in Christ God forgave you.

questions: When you're hurt or angry, what do you usually do first: go quiet, get loud, leave the room, or rush to smooth it over?
What does your partner do in a disagreement that makes it harder for you to stay calm? What do you do that makes it harder for them?
What did you learn growing up about whether it was safe to disagree out loud?
What does a real apology sound like to you? What do you need to hear, and what do you find hardest to say?
Is there a subject you've stopped raising because it isn't worth the fight? Name it here, even if you're not ready to say it aloud.
Have you ever raised your voice, slammed something, or said something cruel to win an argument or end it? What did it cost?
After your worst argument so far, how did you come back to each other? Who went first, and was anything left unsaid?
sessions.together:
Write down how the two of you will fight, and both sign it. Start with these and change what doesn't fit. Big subjects don't get started after ten at night. Either of you can call a pause, but whoever calls it names a time to come back, tomorrow at seven rather than *later*, and keeps it. Take one subject at a time. Don't call names or show contempt, and never threaten to end the engagement or the marriage in the middle of a fight. Neither of you takes a fight to social media, or to your family first. These rules are for disagreements, not fear: if you're ever afraid, tell someone you trust, whatever you agreed.

Then practice on something small, like where to eat or how to spend a Saturday. One of you speaks while the other listens and says back what they heard, until the first says *yes, that's it*. Then switch. It will feel slow, and slow is what the letter of James asks for.

Last, if either of you answered the sixth question with something you're not proud of, say it plainly, without excuses. If it happens often, it's more than a bad habit, and the one doing it should see a licensed counselor before the wedding. If it has ever frightened the other, stop the workbook here, and the one who was afraid should talk alone with someone they trust or call the Hotline.
sessions.practice: The next time you disagree about anything, even something small, use the slow way you practiced. Afterward, each of you tell the other one thing they did that helped. If a fight goes badly, come back to it within a day and finish it, and if you can't get through it on your own, bring it to your pastor or mentor.

sessions.title: Money
sessions.why:
Money fights are rarely about money alone. They're about security and fear, and about what each of you learned at home about whether there would ever be enough. Couples who never talk about money don't avoid the fight. They postpone it until there's a mortgage, a baby, or a debt one of you didn't mention.

So begin with honesty. Before the wedding, put everything on the table: income, debts, credit, spending habits, money you send to family, any gambling. Hidden debt is a broken promise waiting to be found. Decide how decisions will be made before a big one arrives, and whatever you conclude about roles in session seven, neither of you should have money the other can't see. If one of you controls all the money in a way the other can't question, or runs up debt in the other's name, that's control, and it belongs with the warning at the front of this workbook. This session isn't financial advice; for a plan to deal with debt, see a qualified financial counselor.

The prayer in Proverbs 30 belongs to a man named Agur, and it suits two people about to share a bank account. He asks first for honesty, and only then for neither poverty nor riches, because too much might lead him to deny God and too little might lead him to steal. Many marriages meet both dangers, sometimes in different years and sometimes in different spouses. The letter to the Hebrews ties contentment to a promise: God has said he will never leave you. Much of our anxiety about money is a search for that promise somewhere else.

scripture.text: Two things I ask of You— do not refuse me before I die: Keep falsehood and deceitful words far from me. Give me neither poverty nor riches; feed me with the bread that is my portion. Otherwise, I may have too much and deny You, saying, ‘Who is the LORD?’ Or I may become poor and steal, profaning the name of my God.
Keep your lives free from the love of money and be content with what you have, for God has said: “Never will I leave you, never will I forsake you.”

questions: What do you owe, to whom, and at what interest? Write the real numbers, including the ones you'd rather not.
What did money feel like in the home you grew up in: tight, comfortable, secret, or a reason for fights?
What do you spend money on that you'd be tempted to hide, or to describe as less than it is?
Do you send money to family or friends, or expect that you will? How much, and for how long?
What would you want the two of you to give away each year, and to whom?
If your income fell by a quarter next month, what would you cut first, and what would you fight to keep?
Above what amount should neither of you spend without talking to the other first? Why that amount?
sessions.together:
Bring the real papers to this conversation: pay stubs, loan balances, card statements, and a credit report if you've never looked at yours. Read them together without commentary first, then talk about what surprised you.

Next, decide how money will move in your marriage. Whether you keep one account or separate ones is something Scripture doesn't settle, but it does settle honesty, so whatever you choose, both of you should be able to see everything. Agree on the amount from the last question, and on what you'll do first if one of you loses a job.

Then talk about giving. Decide together what you'll give and to whom, and make it a decision rather than whatever is left at the end of the month.

Last, pray Agur's prayer together in your own words, if you're able. If gambling, drinking, or spending is out of hand for either of you, see a licensed counselor before the wedding, and if money is already a weight on you, the page at livewellbyjamesbell.co/help/money may help.
sessions.practice: Each of you write down everything you spend for two weeks, down to the coffee. Then sit together and sketch a rough monthly plan: what comes in, what goes out, what you'll give, what you'll save, and what you'll pay down. Keep it rough. What matters is that you made it together, and that both of you know the truth about your money.

sessions.title: Sex and the body
sessions.why:
Many of us learned about sex from a screen, or from a church that mostly told us what not to do. Some churches said nothing until the wedding and expected a switch to flip. I'm a pastor, so that criticism includes me. The culture talks about sex constantly and makes it cheap. Scripture is neither silent nor cheap about it. It keeps a whole book of love poetry that celebrates desire without embarrassment, and Paul writes about married sex with startling frankness.

Paul gives the wife the same authority over her husband's body that he gives the husband over hers, and tells them not to deprive each other. Every line runs both ways, and what he describes is something each one owes and gives, never something either one takes. These verses have been used to demand sex, which turns them inside out. Consent is never optional, before the wedding or after it. If either of you feels pressured now, stop the workbook and use the help at the front.

You'll each bring a history into marriage: past partners, pornography, a body you're ashamed of, or harm someone did to you. Tell each other the truth that matters before the wedding, without graphic detail; a pastor or counselor can help you decide what needs saying. If someone harmed you sexually, it wasn't your fault, and it doesn't make you any less worth marrying.

Christians of every historic tradition have taught that sex belongs within marriage, and so does living together as a couple. Paul's answer to sexual immorality is marriage, and the Song warns not to awaken love until the time is right. The reason isn't that the body is shameful. Sex makes with the body the promise the vows make with words. If you're already sleeping together or living together, you're not the first, and you're not ruined. Talk with your pastor about what faithfulness looks like from here. The Song says love is as strong as death, and something that strong needs a promise strong enough to hold it.

scripture.text: But because there is so much sexual immorality, each man should have his own wife, and each woman her own husband. The husband should fulfill his marital duty to his wife, and likewise the wife to her husband. The wife does not have authority over her own body, but the husband. Likewise the husband does not have authority over his own body, but the wife. Do not deprive each other, except by mutual consent and for a time, so you may devote yourselves to prayer. Then come together again, so that Satan will not tempt you through your lack of self-control.

O daughters of Jerusalem, I adjure you: Do not arouse or awaken love until the time is right. ... Set me as a seal over your heart, as a seal upon your arm. For love is as strong as death, its jealousy as unrelenting as Sheol. Its sparks are fiery flames, the fiercest blaze of all. Mighty waters cannot quench love; rivers cannot sweep it away. If a man were to give all the wealth of his house for love, his offer would be utterly scorned.

questions: What did you learn about sex growing up, from family, church, friends, or a screen? What do you wish someone had told you instead?
What are you hoping for in your sexual life together, and what are you nervous about?
Is there anything in your sexual history, including pornography, that your partner should hear from you before the wedding rather than discover after it? You don't need to write details here.
If someone has ever harmed you sexually, what would you want your partner to understand? You never have to write what happened.
Is there anything about your health, physical or mental, including your sexual health, that your partner should know before the wedding?
When one of you wants sex and the other doesn't, how do you hope you'll handle it? What would make a no feel safe to say?
What would faithfulness look like for the two of you between now and the wedding?
sessions.together:
This may be the most awkward conversation in the workbook, so sit side by side rather than across a table, and be gentle with each other.

Talk first about your hopes and your nerves, and about how you'll handle it when your desire doesn't match. Then say this to each other out loud, in your own words: either of us can say no, at any time, before the wedding and after it, and the other won't punish, sulk, or pressure. If that sentence is hard for one of you to say, take it to your pastor or a licensed counselor before you go further. If it's hard to believe because the other has pressured you before, stop the workbook and use the help at the front.

Next, talk about the historic teaching in this session and what it means for the two of you before the wedding. If one of you doesn't share the faith, say honestly what you make of it, and listen to why it matters to the other. If you're already sleeping together or living together, make an appointment with your pastor to talk about next steps.

If the third question brought something to the surface, decide together who you'll ask for help, and when; for pornography, start with livewellbyjamesbell.co/help/pornography. If the fourth did, the one who was harmed chooses what help to seek, and when. A licensed counselor can help at your own pace, and RAINN is in the box at the front.
sessions.practice: Each of you read the Song of Songs on your own. It's eight short chapters of love poetry, and some of it is frank. Notice that both lovers speak and both delight, and tell each other one line that surprised you. If anything from tonight needs help, make that call this week rather than waiting until after the wedding.

sessions.title: Roles, work, and children
sessions.why:
Who does what in a marriage used to be settled by custom. Now couples work it out as they go, and resentment gathers around whoever ends up with the dishes or the night feedings. Underneath the chores is a question about husbands and wives, and faithful Christians read Ephesians 5 in two main ways.

Complementarians hold that God made men and women equal in dignity and distinct in role, and that this passage teaches a lasting pattern: the husband leads by giving himself up as Christ did, and the wife willingly submits to him as the church submits to Christ. They note that the letter grounds this in Christ and the church and in Genesis 2, not in Roman custom, and that the heavier command falls on the husband, who must love even to death. Their comfort is a clear shape for the home and a husband who answers to God for how he loves.

Egalitarians hold that men and women are equal in dignity and in authority, and that the first line, submit to one another out of reverence for Christ, governs the rest. They read the letter's words to wives as working inside the household order of its day while changing it from within, much as its words to slaves a chapter later regulated a practice without endorsing it. They point to Galatians 3:28 and to a head who nourishes and cherishes the body. Their comfort is a marriage where both lead and both yield, and gifts, not gender, decide the tasks.

Both readings agree that a husband's love must be costly, that the passage gives no cover to control or abuse, and that you stand before Christ as equals. This question divides faithful churches without dividing anyone from Christ. Settle it with your pastor and your church.

scripture.text: Submit to one another out of reverence for Christ. Wives, submit to your husbands as to the Lord. For the husband is the head of the wife as Christ is the head of the church, His body, of which He is the Savior. Now as the church submits to Christ, so also wives should submit to their husbands in everything. Husbands, love your wives, just as Christ loved the church and gave Himself up for her to sanctify her, cleansing her by the washing with water through the word, and to present her to Himself as a glorious church, without stain or wrinkle or any such blemish, but holy and blameless. In the same way, husbands ought to love their wives as their own bodies. He who loves his wife loves himself. Indeed, no one ever hated his own body, but he nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ does the church. For we are members of His body. “For this reason a man will leave his father and mother and be united to his wife, and the two will become one flesh.” This mystery is profound, but I am speaking about Christ and the church. Nevertheless, each one of you also must love his wife as he loves himself, and the wife must respect her husband.

Unless the LORD builds the house, its builders labor in vain; unless the LORD protects the city, its watchmen stand guard in vain. In vain you rise early and stay up late, toiling for bread to eat— for He gives sleep to His beloved. Children are indeed a heritage from the LORD, and the fruit of the womb is His reward.

questions: Who did what in the home you grew up in: cooking, bills, discipline, decisions? What do you want to keep, and what do you want to change?
Reading Ephesians 5:21-33, which words are hardest for you to hear, and why?
When the two of you can't agree and a decision has to be made, how do you think it should be settled?
Do you want children? How many, and when? Write what you actually want, not what you've agreed to so far.
If you learned you couldn't have children together, what would you want to do, and what would you be afraid of?
If one of you were offered a job that meant moving, or one job began to swallow the marriage, how would you decide what to do?
Besides marrying this person, what do you believe you're meant to do with your life? How will your marriage make room for it?
sessions.together:
Start with the second and third questions. If you read Ephesians 5 differently, take it to your pastor now, before your first hard decision.

Read Psalm 127 aloud; it puts your work, your house, and your children in God's hands before yours. Then talk about whether you want children and when. Christians differ on birth control. The Catholic Church and some Protestants hold that married love should stay open to new life, because God joined love and new life from the beginning (Genesis 1:28) and children are his gift; Catholic teaching allows spacing births by natural means for just reasons. Their comfort is trusting God with a family's size and timing. Many Protestants hold that a couple may use birth control wisely, finding no command against it and noting that Paul's frank words on married sex say nothing about children (1 Corinthians 7:3-5), though many of them refuse any method they believe could end a life already conceived. Their comfort is freedom to plan as stewards. Both receive children as a gift and ask husband and wife to decide together. Ask a doctor how each method works, and settle this with your pastor and your church.

Last, talk about what you'd do if children don't come. When Hannah wept over her empty years, her husband asked whether he wasn't better to her than ten sons (1 Samuel 1:8); he loved her and still missed her grief. If that grief becomes yours, livewellbyjamesbell.co/help/infertility was written for it.
sessions.practice: Divide the work of your future home on paper, the chores and the bills. Then spend two weeks noticing who actually does that kind of work now, wherever you live and whenever you're together, and whether your list is honest about it. Make an appointment with your pastor or mentor to talk through Ephesians 5 and birth control, and bring your answers to the second and third questions. If you found tonight that you want different things about children, take that too, and don't treat it as settled either way.

sessions.title: The vows
sessions.why:
Soon you'll stand in front of people who love you and say words you can't take back. The old vows, in the form many couples still use, promise faithfulness for better and for worse, for richer and for poorer, in sickness and in health, until death parts you. People often say them through tears and hardly hear them. This session is for hearing them before you say them.

Ecclesiastes is speaking of vows made to God, and it's blunt: it's better not to vow than to vow and not keep it. Wedding vows are made in his presence, and the warning is there to give them their real weight. A vow is a promise about a future neither of you can see, made to a person you'll keep discovering, including parts of them you didn't choose. Psalm 15 asks who may dwell with God, and part of its answer is the one who keeps a costly oath.

The measure of the promise is Christ. The letter to the Ephesians tells its readers to walk in love as Christ loved us and gave himself up for us, and in the same chapter tells husbands to love their wives that way. First Corinthians 13 is read at a great many weddings, but Paul wrote it to a quarreling church, and much of it describes what love does when it's tired, slighted, or wronged.

*For worse* covers illness, failure, grief, poverty, and the years when the feeling goes quiet. It doesn't mean staying within reach of harm. Love takes no pleasure in evil, and the one who makes the other afraid is the one who breaks the vow. None of us keeps a vow by willpower. We keep it because God keeps his covenant with us, and we keep it the way forgiven people do, by coming back, confessing, forgiving, and beginning again, for the rest of our lives.

scripture.text: When you make a vow to God, do not delay in fulfilling it, because He takes no pleasure in fools. Fulfill your vow. It is better not to vow than to make a vow and not fulfill it.
Be imitators of God, therefore, as beloved children, and walk in love, just as Christ loved us and gave Himself up for us as a fragrant sacrificial offering to God.

Love is patient, love is kind. It does not envy, it does not boast, it is not proud. It is not rude, it is not self-seeking, it is not easily angered, it keeps no account of wrongs. Love takes no pleasure in evil, but rejoices in the truth. It bears all things, believes all things, hopes all things, endures all things.

questions: Which words of the vows will be easiest for you to say? Which will be hardest, and why?
What might *for worse* actually look like for the two of you? Name something specific.
What are you about to promise that you aren't sure you can keep?
Is there anything you need to tell your partner before the wedding, so that you don't make your vows with something hidden?
When you fail each other, as you will, what do you want the way back to look like?
Who will you ask to hold you to these promises, and what exactly will you ask them to do?
If you could add one sentence to your vows in your own words, what would you most want to promise?
sessions.together:
Read aloud the vows you plan to say, at home and slowly, not at the rehearsal. After each line, stop, and each of you say one concrete thing it would mean in an ordinary year. Then trade answers to the third and fourth questions. If you've been hiding something you've done, tonight is the night to say it; if it's too heavy for the two of you, take it to your pastor. Harm done to you is different; you can tell it in your own time, with help.

Then talk about your witnesses. The people at a wedding are more than an audience. They're there to see you promise, and some of them should be people who will ask you, years from now, how you're keeping it. Choose two, a couple or two friends who know you both, and decide what you'll ask of them.

Last, if you're able, pray together, or sit together quietly for a minute. Then each of you finish this sentence aloud: *When we're old, I hope it's true of us that...*
sessions.practice: There's no ninth session, unless you count your first anniversary. Before the wedding, go over your vows line by line with the person who will marry you, and ask the two witnesses you chose to hold you to them. Then, on your first anniversary, open this workbook again and answer what you can without looking at what you wrote the first time. Compare afterward.
